opening.headline: Before considering tuning, learn criteria to determine how far you can go with improved prompting and when you've reached your limits.
body: If the format keeps getting wrong, many teams immediately think of tuning. But if you only have one line of prompts, there's still a lot to check before choosing the expensive route.

In this lesson, we'll look at how three tools can solve problems: clear instructions, examples, and output structures. We then compare the output before and after the improvement and identify what signals the limits of the prompt.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Improved prompts can illustrate the types of problems for which it is effective.
Can distinguish signs of limitations in prompt improvement

screens.title: How far will the prompt go before tuning?
screens.lead: This is a scene where a team is discussing the introduction of tuning. Read carefully what the team's starting point is.

visual.alt: A scene where a dialogue bubble asking to start tuning and a one-line prompt card are placed side by side.
labels: Since the format error is recurring, let's start tuning.

paragraphs: One team is running the summary function. As the response format changes each time, one team member says: Since the format error is recurring, let's start tuning now.

However, when I open the current prompt, there is only one line, 'Summary.' There's no telling me to summarize in what format, in how many lines, or for whom, and there are no examples of good summaries. This is a situation where you are trying to choose an expensive route without checking how far it is possible through the prompt.

OpenAI's accuracy optimization guide suggests that prompt engineering is often the best starting point. This is because there are many tasks, such as summarization, translation, and code generation, that reach working-level accuracy and consistency by simply asking for instructions without examples.

This class covers two things: What problems are solved by prompts, and what are the signals that prompts have reached their limits? You must be able to distinguish between these two so that you can provide a basis when moving on to tuning.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: Can I base my tuning decisions on failures from one-line prompts? I will outline what signals there should be at the end of class.

screens.outro: Now let me first think about your experience.

screens.title: Think about how many times you changed the prompt
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't have to enter or submit your answer, so think about your own experience first and then click on it.

items.prompt: How many times have you tried improving your prompts before stopping?
items.answer: There are many cases where people try to fix something once or twice and then stop because it doesn't work. But that number alone doesn't tell you whether you've reached your limit. It is more important to keep a record of what has been changed and by what standards it has improved.

items.prompt: Was the reason you stopped because ‘enough is enough’ or ‘I can’t do more’?
items.answer: The two reasons are completely different. It means that the standard of 'enough is enough' has been met, and it is a judgment that must be considered to see whether it is a limit signal that 'no more can be done'. This class covers how to check the latter through evaluation results rather than intuition.

items.prompt: What did you change at that time: instructions, examples, or output format?
items.answer: There is a possibility that you may have tried to focus on just one thing. You can either keep writing long instructions or increase examples. Since these three solve different problems, it's useful to check which one you haven't tried yet.

screens.outro: Now that we've summarized our experience, let's check out the three tools Prompt uses one by one.

screens.title: Three effective tools: instructions, examples, and output structure.
screens.lead: Select each tab to compare what problems each tool solves and how bad and improved examples differ.

visual.alt: Clear instructions, examples, and output structure Three columns of cards with illustrations comparing the text before and after improvement on each card.
labels: Summarize a customer inquiry in two sentences
Three input and expected output pairs
Separate instructions, context, examples, and input into tags

tabs.label: clear instructions
tabs.body:
**Problem solved**: When the goal of the desired output is ambiguous and the model fills in guesses.

**Bad example**: 'Summary'

**Improvement example**: ‘Read one customer inquiry and summarize the key complaints and requests in two sentences. 'Use specific expressions so that the person in charge can take action immediately.'

Anthropic's prompt guide tells you to write clearly and directly. Telling the model specifically what you want it for, for whom, and how you want it to look is the most basic and cheapest improvement.

tabs.label: Example(few-shot)
tabs.body:
**Problem solved**: When you need to demonstrate a response style or tone that is difficult to explain in words.

**How ​​to**: Putting a few correct input and output pairs into a prompt is called a few-shot. The model infers from the examples how it should respond.

**Note**: Anthropic documentation recommends choosing relevant, varied examples and structuring them with `<example>` tags. If you only add similar examples, the model will only follow the shape.

It is common for a few examples to solve formatting problems where verbal instructions did not work.

tabs.label: output structure
tabs.body:
**Problem solved**: Instructions, references, examples, and user input are all mixed together and the model misunderstands the role of each.

**How ​​to**: Write instructions, context, examples, and input divided into XML tags. For example, `<instructions>`, `<context>`, `<input>`. According to the Anthropic documentation, this division reduces the potential for the model to misinterpret content.

You can frame your response in the same way. Specifying what you want the output to look like with tags or formats also makes subsequent processing of the results easier.

tabs.label: Context is also one axis.
tabs.body:
Directions and formats are not the only things covered by prompts. Information that the model did not learn can also be entered directly into the prompt. When you paste the necessary data, the model looks at the data and answers.

However, if the information exceeds the input size or varies from question to question, it is difficult to contain it in a static prompt. That limitation is why we will consider search augmentation later. The three tools on this screen address Instructions, Examples, and Structure, and the issue of information volume is addressed again in the Limit Signals screen.

screens.outro: Now that you know the tool, let's compare before and after improvements to see how the output actually changes.

screens.title: Comparing output before and after improvement: Examples change behavior
screens.lead: Select the two states alternately and compare the results before and after improvement of the same task. Think about how the results change and what that change tells you.

visual.alt: A bar graph comparing the results of an attempt without an example and the results after an example.
labels: Task: Correcting Icelandic sentences with errors using as few words as possible

states.label: Before improvement: No examples
states.body:
**Task**: Take an Icelandic sentence with errors and return the corrected sentence with minimal word changes. The system instructions are: 'Correct sentences that may contain errors with as few word changes as possible.'

**Results**: In the first attempt, where only instructions were given without examples, the BLEU value, which measures translation quality, was 62. It's not a bad start, but it's hard to get a feel for how much the model needs to be modified just from the input.

**Interpretation**: This value becomes the baseline against which all future improvements will be compared. You need a baseline so you can say whether the next change worked.

states.label: After improvement: added example
states.body:
**Change**: Added three static few-shot examples of sentences with errors and pairs of corrected sentences below the system instructions. This method involves showing the model instead of explaining it in words.

**Result**: BLEU value increased from 62 to 70. This is a BLEU increase of 8 points, and the relative increase based on 62 is approximately 12.9%.

**Interpretation**: This document interprets that the model already had the knowledge to solve the problem, and what was lacking was action. So in this case, the next candidate is one that shows more examples rather than adding new information. The fact that it rose significantly with just one additional example was a clue that the cause was action.

screens.outro: Now that we have identified the areas that can be solved with one improvement, let's take a look at how to distinguish between limit signals.

screens.title: Commentary: Distinguish between solvable problems and signs of limitations
screens.lead: The instructor demonstrates how to adjudicate a case using three questions. Select the right arrow to skip a step. You will not enter an answer.

steps.title: read the case
steps.body: One team created a feature that turns a product description into a three-line summary. Sometimes the summary is two lines, sometimes it is five lines. The prompt is ‘Summary.’ The team is considering tuning.

steps.title: Question 1: Are the instructions ambiguous?
steps.body: Currently the prompt has no giver, no object, and no format. The instructions are ambiguous, so the model is guessing. This is a problem solved with a prompt. If you write something like ‘summarize in three lines and write each line as one sentence’, it is likely to be resolved at this stage.

steps.title: Question 2: Is this an example?
steps.body: If your tone or line length is jagged even after you've refined your instructions, here's an example: Show two or three good summaries with your input. Remember that there are many tasks that can be done at a practical level with a zero-shot approach, such as summarization, translation, and code generation. There are many problems to be solved at this stage as well.

steps.title: Question 3: Is it a matter of quantity of information?
steps.body: If you make a mistake even after providing instructions and examples, this time check whether the necessary information is included in the input. If the information needed exceeds the input scale or varies from question to question and cannot be contained in a static prompt, this is a sign of limitations. In this case, we're looking at searches that dynamically supply context that matches the question.

steps.title: Limiting signal number two: Prompts just get longer
steps.body: If increasing the examples doesn't lead to more consistent behavior and the prompts just keep getting longer, this is also a sign of limitations. At this point, you can look at tuning to train on even more examples. Increasing length but not increasing coherence may mean that the prompt has done all it can.

steps.title: Basis for Judgment: Assessment Set
steps.body: The basis for all these decisions is not a feeling, but a set of evaluations. The OpenAI document identifies the best output of the prompt stage as having more than 20 questions and standard answers, looking at failures and forming hypotheses about the cause. This case is determined to be a problem solved in question 1, so tuning is still too early.

screens.outro: Now that you know how to recognize the limit signal, let's organize the next lever to select after the prompt reaches the limit.

screens.title: Prompt scale limits and next lever
screens.lead: The table below shows which lever to move to depending on the signal when the prompt reaches the limit. Read each line from left to right.

data.caption: Limit signal and next lever
rows: The information needed exceeds the input size or varies from question to question and cannot be contained in a static prompt.
Context. The input does not contain information that the model needs to know.
Search that dynamically supplies context tailored to your question
The evaluation set verifies that the material needed for the top results is actually coming in.
Increasing the number of examples does not result in more consistent behavior and only makes the prompts longer.
action. The model does not reliably follow the method.
Check whether you can collect enough examples of correct answers and whether there are evaluation criteria.
The format is shaky due to vague instructions or lack of examples.
Not yet the limit. Prompts are less polished
Continue improving prompts without going to the next lever
Check whether any of the instructions, examples, and output structures contain tools that have not yet been used.
data.notes: The OpenAI documentation explains that prompt engineering often does not scale well at scale. Limitations emerge when you need to supply dynamic context or require more consistent behavior than what you get from examples. Either way, you'll first determine the cause of the failure through assessment before making your choice, and don't skip getting a baseline because prompting is the cheapest first step. If you mistake a case that is not already a limit for a limit, as in the third row of the table, you will end up going down an expensive path before you can sufficiently refine your prompt. Conversely, if the signals in the first and second rows are repeatedly identified in the evaluation, it makes sense to stop writing longer prompts and prepare for the next lever. This judgment should always be made using the same set of assessments to ensure a fair comparison before and after improvement.

screens.outro: On the last screen, I will summarize the principles of today's order.

screens.title: Prompt is the cheapest first step
screens.lead: We will summarize the class by answering the first question, whether it is okay to start tuning right away, using the standards learned today.

paragraphs: In the first scene, the team was discussing tuning with the one-line prompt ‘Summary.’ Now I can explain why that judgment was premature. This is because failures that occur when instructions are vague and there are no examples are likely to be resolved by improving the prompts.

There are three key tools in Prompt: Clear instructions make your goals concrete. The example shows a response that is difficult to explain in words. Output structure reduces misunderstandings by distinguishing between instructions, context, examples, and input.

If one improvement makes a big difference, it's likely a behavioral issue. As with the Icelandic correction example, the fact that the BLEU value went from 62 to 70 with just a few examples is a clue that the model already had the knowledge.

Conversely, when limitations in the amount of information or consistency are repeated, the next path is reviewed. If information is not included in the input, look for search, and if consistency does not improve even if you increase the examples, look for tuning. In both cases, the evaluation set is the basis for the judgment.

In summary, prompts are the cheapest first step, and the assessment set and baseline you create during this step is what all your subsequent choices will be compared against. You can check whether the limit has been reached by measuring, not by feeling.

In practice, this order is applied as follows: First, check whether the current prompt has exhausted its instructions, examples, and output structures. Next, measure the baseline by creating around 20 questions and baseline answers. Finally, record any remaining failures divided into information problems and behavioral problems. This record will provide a basis for any tuning or search suggestions.

callout.label: Based on one sentence
callout.text: Prompting is the cheapest first step, and it is only when the limits of information volume and consistency are reached that we move on to search and tuning.

checks.intro: Check for yourself by recalling the before-and-after comparison of the improvements you just saw. Results are not recorded.
checks.q: In the Icelandic language proofreading work, I added only a few static examples and the results improved significantly. What do these results imply?
options: The knowledge needed for the model was already there, what was lacking was action.
The model acquired new, unlearned knowledge through examples.
There is no room for further improvement in the prompt method.
It is immediately necessary to attach external documents to the search
checks.correctFeedback: That's correct. A large increase based on examples alone is a clue that there is a lack of action, not knowledge.
checks.incorrectFeedback: It is difficult to interpret it that way. Recall what examples are tools for change.
checks.explain: Significant improvement based on examples alone means that the knowledge was already there and the method of answering was the problem. So the one who shows more examples becomes the next candidate.

wrong.1: Examples are a tool for inferring how to respond, not a means of introducing new knowledge.
wrong.2: Rather, the improvement was significant, showing that there is room for prompts.
wrong.3: Since a lack of information has not been revealed, there is no basis to believe that a search is necessary.

checks.intro: Think of the three questions you saw in the commentary and pair them with the situation and judgment. Results are not recorded.
checks.q: Match the situation with the right decision
left: The instructions are vague and there are no examples, so the format is shaky.
The information needed is different every time, making it difficult to include in a static prompt.
Even if you increase the examples, consistency does not improve and the prompts only become longer.
right: Review searches that dynamically supply context
Problems that are likely to be solved by improving prompts
Review tuning that trains with many examples
checks.correctFeedback: All three situations were associated with appropriate judgments.
checks.incorrectFeedback: Some pairs were mismatched. Again, try to determine if the information is lacking, if the behavior is shaky, or if the prompt is less polished.
checks.explain: Problems solved by prompts and limit signals are distinguished. Limits on the information side lead to search, and limits on the action side lead to tuning.

checks.intro: Lastly, check the reason for the order. Results are not recorded.
checks.q: What is the best reason to recommend prompt engineering before tuning?
options: Because prompts always scale well with scale.
Because tuning doesn't solve format problems at all.
Because it is the cheapest first step and provides a baseline for comparing future improvements.
Because prompts solve any lack of information problem.
checks.correctFeedback: That's right. The reason for the order is that it has the lowest cost and creates a baseline.
checks.incorrectFeedback: The reason is not true. Recall the strengths and limitations of the prompt.
checks.explain: Prompting is the lowest cost first step, and you need a baseline to judge the effectiveness of the next lever.

wrong.0: Rather, the documentation explains that prompts often do not scale well with scale.
wrong.1: Tuning does a good job of addressing formal issues, but costs money and preparation, so it comes second.
wrong.3: When information exceeds the input volume, prompts alone have limitations.

glossary.def: A technique that shows how to respond by adding several examples of correct input and output to a prompt.
This is a method of requesting only instructions without examples. There are many tasks that reach a practical level even with zero shots, such as summarization or translation.
XML tags or formatting are used to separate instructions, context, examples, and frames between input and response.
It is a set of questions and standard answers that serve as a basis for measuring improvement each time you change the prompt.

misconceptions.myth: Prompts are a temporary solution, the real improvement is tuning.
misconceptions.fact: Tasks like summarization, translation, and code generation often reach working-level accuracy and consistency with just prompts. Prompt is the cheapest first step.

misconceptions.myth: The more examples you include, the better.
misconceptions.fact: Relevance and variety of examples are more important than number. If consistency does not improve even if you increase the examples and the prompts become longer, then consider a different route.

misconceptions.myth: Longer prompts are a sign that improvement is taking place.
misconceptions.fact: If consistency does not increase with length, it is a sign of limitation. It should be judged by the results of the evaluation, not the length.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Prompt is the cheapest first step.
Many of the formal issues are addressed first, with clear instructions, examples, and output structures.
If one improvement makes a big difference, it's likely a behavioral issue.
When the limits of information volume and consistency become repetitive, we move on to search or tuning.

closing.reflection: As we improve our prompts, what signals can we see that tell us we're reaching our limits?
